segments.title: THE ACT THAT COMES FIRST
notes: Focus On One Thing (No Shiny Object Syndrome)
Embodiment - Be Who You Strive To Be
segments.angle: What is the fundamental problem or need that this note/idea is trying to address? Is it addressing a symptom or the root cause? (Think: Five Whys)

sources.text: Embodiment - Be Who You Strive To Be: Character is built not through words, but through actions and behaviours. Do not merely pretend; become.

Embodiment - Be Who You Strive To Be: Mental patients were asked to fill in a personality test acting as if they were a “typical, well-adjusted person”. In order for these patients to answer the questions “as a typical, well-adjusted person” would answer, they had to imagine how a typical well-adjusted person would act.
Focus On One Thing: You don’t lack direction. You have too many directions. An open mind, like an open mouth, needs to eventually close on something.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Somewhere in your house there's an envelope. On the back, in your own handwriting, is the person you'd be if this year went well.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every household has a drawer for good intentions, stuffed with a lost stamp and a few plans nobody read again. The fellow you wish to be is usually in there somewhere.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Where he couldn't embarrass you. You have to feel ready before you start. That's the lie we all tell.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Say it properly, March. Let the lie speak in its own voice, so we may both take a swing at it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Wait until the courage arrives. Then move.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Wait, says the lie, feet up on the stool.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now the note, which disagrees with the lie in plain type. Hear it: “Character is built not through words, but through actions and behaviours.” The best of it is further down. I'm keeping it back, like the last biscuit in the tin.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the feeling is what comes after. Not what leads the way.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes. The feeling turns up after the walking, like a cat that waits until you've sat down before it climbs into your lap.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Try it on a woman with a biro and a biscuit tin on her windowsill. She's been asked to fill in a personality form. She has to answer as the calm, well-adjusted version of herself.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Mind the form. She can't tick calm until she knows what calm would do with its hands. That's the whole trick of the study, March. They had to imagine the sort of person who would answer.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So she imagines a calm woman's hands. Does she lift the tin lid?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: She lifts the lid, takes out the one biscuit she was saving, and wonders whether a calm woman would eat it now or after the form.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: She eats it now. Small act. It counts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The lid, the biscuit, a pen uncapped. Each is a small act a well-adjusted woman would do without consulting the clock, and that's exactly what the form was asking her to find out.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Question one. She answers without looking at the clock.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And by the later questions her hand has stopped shaking over the page. Nobody handed her courage. She merely behaved, and the courage crept in behind her, sheepish, like a guest who arrives after the party's started and pretends he was invited.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the proof is the sequence. The act comes, then the steadier hand.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Let me try it on myself, out loud. The calm me closes the drawer. Does the small thing at the top of the list. Stops checking the time.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I'd answer that form yes. Every question.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: How simple. Any child with a biscuit tin could manage it before breakfast.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't call it simple.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple's what people say when they've never done it at midnight, with the kettle gone cold.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ouch. Cold kettle, noted.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I withdraw simple, and offer difficult. Grander. You'll like it even less.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Grander is worse.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I'm not sure I like either. The honest answer is I'd want the envelope back before anything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Look up, March. A crow has landed on the radio mast on the hill, the very mast we've been insulting all night. A sign, if ever there was one. The mast was built to send messages, and the crow has chosen to receive one.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a crow on the highest thing on the hill. That's all the mast is, narrator. Highest point, best view for a bird.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Destiny is only the highest point, March, and I'm standing at the bottom of it, where the view is best.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. You can have the crow. I'm putting it on my tally...

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: In a column I'm not allowed to see. You've taken the crow, the tally and the last of the biscuits. I'm lodging a complaint with the mast. It won't be answered, which is how I like my complaints.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Back to the claim, then. Why do people jump to the next shiny thing? Ask why until it stops.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Because the next one looks easier. Why does it look easier?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Because the one in hand hasn't yet turned into them.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And why hasn't it? That's the root, isn't it. The root is the person, not the model.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The model is merely a leaf, March. The tree is the person. And the root is that he was never built to stay, because nobody showed him how staying begins.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So focus names the habit you need to resist. Embodiment names the person who does the resisting.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: “You don’t lack direction. You have too many directions.” Focus names the problem. Embodiment names the one who has to change. Without him, the naming is no use.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Neither shows it alone. Focus alone says stop chasing. Embodiment alone says become someone, with no idea what to stop.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the fix doesn't begin in the next tab. It begins in the way you act, and the person you act as. A far less comfortable place to start.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's the fork. Someone who believes this has a kitchen table, a page at the top that says I finish things, and a small finishing act before they open anything new.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A kitchen table. Go on, I'm listening.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Put the lid back on. Rinse the mug. Close the letter. The act is the proof. The feeling arrives later, almost by accident.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Accident, then, which is how the best habits in the old stories always turn up, once the hero stops waiting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Which is a gentler way of saying you act first and wait for the feeling to catch up.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Gentler, yes, though you were blunter at the start. You are tiresome, March.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now fetch the envelope from the drawer. Don't open it yet. Just look at the handwriting.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Very well. The letters are smaller now, March, and steadier, like a man who's taken to finishing his sentences. I concede, grudgingly, that you were right. The act came first.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I didn't hear that. Don't say it again.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I wasn't delighted, March. I was merely tired. This is what happens when you keep a man up past the stool's bedtime.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's the small hours, the kettle's on, and you're pretending not to be pleased. Up next, the notes on Novelty - A Life Fully Lived and The Influence Of Others. Bring the tin.

segments.title: THE CORD THAT SOLD
segments.angle: How would this idea change if it had to be implemented on a completely different platform (e.g., physical product -> digital service, individual tool -> community platform)?

sources.text: The Value of Time: Time magnifies the margin between success & failure.
Any Benefit Fallacy: Not every beneficial activity or habit is worth your time.
Any Benefit Fallacy: Just because something offers any positive outcome doesn't justify its pursuit.
The Value of Time: It will multiply whatever you feed it. Good habits make time your ally. Bad habits make time your enemy.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Somewhere this week there's an hour you can't account for. The spice jars got sorted, the fridge got wiped. By midnight you felt busy.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A lovely hour, lost in a tin of good intentions.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Which is the worst part.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before I open the note, the lie gets its say. Most people believe any beneficial habit is worth adding. More good things can only help. Say it, March, like a man at a wedding with a glass in his hand.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: More good things can only help. So add the spice jars, the stretching, the fridge. Why not add everything?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Why not, indeed. The lie hands out habits like sweets at a fair, and everybody leaves with a bag.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then what does the note say, exactly?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It disagrees in plain type: “Not every beneficial activity or habit is worth your time.” The whole argument follows, but the best of it I'm keeping back... like the final spoon of sauce, until the story has earned it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So you're saying a good habit can still be a waste of an evening.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Precisely. The habit can be good, and the hour can still go missing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Goodness is a quality of the habit. Time is what the habit spends.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. Show me, then. Put it on a person, and make it ordinary.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Very well. From an old book with its spine held together by tape comes Odo, a rope-maker. Each evening, Odo twisted one fathom of twine by the lamp, and called that the whole of his trade. Then, in another tale, a ledger turns up. It records that Odo polished every hook in his shed each week, until the iron gleamed like church brass.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Which of those hours paid? Be quick, narrator.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The lamp's hot, March, and the iron was lovely. Every piece shone, and Odo would stand back like a painter admiring a finished sky.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Lovely doesn't buy bread.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Lovely keeps a man's hands from going idle. That's its own kind of wage.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Read me the ledger, then.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here's the bit I kept back. The ledger says the twine sold. A fathom at a time, bundled and carried down to the carters at the harbour. Every hook Odo polished sold nothing at all. Not one of them left the shed.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the polishing was a good habit that paid nothing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Exactly. A gleaming hook is a good thing. It simply wasn't the thing that paid.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the dull bit, the twine, was what kept him fed.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The twine, which I called dull at the start. I stand by that word. I stand by the rope as well.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's a question I can't get out of my head. Did Odo feed his dog before he twisted the twine, or after?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: March, you've wandered into the question of priorities, which is the gravest question in any old book. Before, of course. The bowl first, then the rope.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Why does that matter?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Because a dog that's been fed doesn't bark at the lamp, and a barking dog takes the whole evening.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fair enough.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The bowl sits by the shed door, a round wooden ring. From the lane it looks like the first letter of his name. Destiny, March. Destiny in a dog's dinner.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a bowl, narrator. Nobody spelled anything in it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I credit the bowl with what it did. It was the one small habit that kept the rest of his day from coming undone.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Yes. That's the useful bit. Feeding the dog takes no hours at all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It stops the whole evening unravelling. A good habit worth keeping, and it's cheap.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Cheap, and then you'll tell me the shine was cheap too.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The hooks weren't cheap. They ate the evenings. The bowl ate nothing but dinner.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Back to the crossing, then, since you've dragged me back to the bench.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Time gives the bright side: it will multiply whatever you feed it, and good habits make time your ally. The other note gives the warning. Not every good habit deserves the hours.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Put them side by side and the warning is hiding in the first note too.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So feeding the hooks multiplies nothing useful.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It multiplies the polish, March. A lovely multiplication that buys no bread at the harbour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So here's what neither note shows alone. Time compounds, but only on the right inputs.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Feed the twine and by year's end you have rope the carters want. Feed the hooks and you have a shed that gleams and nothing to sell.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The polish grows every week, and that is the trap. A habit can compound beautifully and still be a waste.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ouch.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Neither note says that alone.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. The Time note on its own sounds like stack up the good habits. The other sounds like cut them down. Together you pick the habit that compounds on the thing that sells.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now put Odo on a platform. A feed, a community of makers, where each person posts a hook, a polish, a length of rope, all in the same small square with the same little heart underneath.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Someone scrolls past a hundred tidy posts to find the one that sold.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A feed of hooks, March. Gleaming, shining, and nobody counts the carters.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's the picture. Whoever believes this has to decide which posts to follow and which to mute.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The rope gets followed. The polish gets muted, gently, a little more every week.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A mute button is a sort of mercy, I suppose.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Or a little crown for whoever presses it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A crown. It's a button, narrator, not a coronation.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then tell me what you hid in the design, March. There's a secret stair in there. Admit it. A tunnel under the feed, with a hook at the bottom that catches the strongest post.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: There's no stair, just a button.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And don't you dare call a button clever.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Too late.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I'll call it clever all the same. It's round, like Odo's dog bowl by the shed. The circle keeps turning up, March, and you keep pretending it's a coincidence.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a circle because circles are easy to press. Stop finding him in everything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Let me end where we began, with the envelope in the drawer. On the back, the person you'd be if the year went well. Tell me, would that fellow polish the hooks, or twist the twine?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, you're right. Twine.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I heard that. Short words, and a concession packed inside them.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't frame it. Change of subject.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Past midnight, and there's still a biscuit tin on the windowsill. Is anyone eating from it?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The tin is empty, March, except for the one saved biscuit, and it's sulking in the corner.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next, the rest of Odo's ledger, the sum at the bottom, and what the hooks cost in the end.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The crow on the radio mast takes the last word, and I shall take it up with the mast. Caw.

segments.title: THE FILTER BEFORE THE ENGINE
segments.angle: How exactly does this idea achieve its proposed outcome? Break down the process step-by-step. Where are the weakest links or assumptions in that process?

sources.text: The Value of Time: Time magnifies the margin between success & failure. It will multiply whatever you feed it. Good habits make time your ally. Bad habits make time your enemy.
Any Benefit Fallacy: Not every beneficial activity or habit is worth your time.
Any Benefit Fallacy: Create criteria to evaluate opportunities before committing to them.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A habit that has never once sold anything, and you feed it every evening anyway. Like a lamp you forgot was lit. You know which one. Not the twine.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, March, you open with the lamp, and I'll allow it. Now let the lie have its turn, as is proper. The lie says once a good habit is started, time takes over and does the rest. Feed the thing, and the hours will do the sums by themselves. Say it the way a grandmother says grace.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Feed it, and the hours do the sums. So I just start. And wait?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Start, and wait. The years stack up behind you like a good harvest in a barn. Nobody has to count it. That's the comfort of the thing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nobody counts it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nobody counts it, March.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's the lie, narrator. A very warm one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then here is the claim, read whole from the note: 'It will multiply whatever you feed it.' Time is the great multiplier, and it doesn't ask what you hand it across the counter.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So it multiplies the polish just as faithfully as the rope.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Just as faithfully. Time has no opinion about the thing it multiplies. It only has a clock.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And the sentence leaves out the carters. It says the feeding gets multiplied. Nothing about bread.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It leaves out the bread, March. I think that's the rudest silence in the whole notebook. Go on, then. Put yourself on the bench.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bread. Finally, someone says it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. This week, out loud, on me. My page. The spice jars, close to an hour. The fridge, wiped down and then wiped again. Stretching every morning. The kettle on before the hour is out... and cold by the time I notice.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And the envelope from the drawer, propped against the teapot where I can't avoid it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A proper page, March. Each line a little altar. The spice jars are a sacred order, and I won't hear them mocked.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then test the sacred order. Does the jar line reach a carter? No. The fridge? No. Stretching? No. Only the envelope asks the question, and it's been sitting by the teapot going cold.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The method is simple. List the habits, ask the question, draw a line through the no answers. The ritual stays. The fridge stays, as practical. And the rope is merely practical too.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple? You've just called the hardest part simple.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Well, that's a bruise.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The next step is the question itself, and the question is easy.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Easy. Which of these is the twine? I can't tell. I'd have to feed one habit for a month before I found out it was the hooks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you'll have polished a month away, March, and I won't soften it. Some of the habits you love are the hooks. Nobody can take them off you but you, and most people never do. The clock won't say a word about it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The clock keeps quiet. The bill arrives later.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And that's the thing I keep turning over. A habit can be perfectly consistent and perfectly wasted.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The same hour compounds the hooks as faithfully as the rope. A fathom of twine and a gleaming hook grow at the same rate in the clock's sums.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't drift off into the clock. Stay on the bench. You're not saying anything new, just making it grander.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I'm saying the clock is indifferent. That is the whole danger. Every hour you spend is counted the same, whether it sells or not.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then here's the hinge. The whole method only works if you already know which habit is the twine before you start. Nobody writes that down.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes. The whole thing hangs on that and nothing else.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nobody ever does.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And you won't know it, March, until the hooks have cost you a month.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the note never says how to check that in advance. It says what multiplies, and what to filter, and leaves the check to whoever's holding the pencil.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The first note is the engine and the other is the filter. The filter has to run before the engine starts, or the engine grinds up whatever the polish hands it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Neither note shows that alone. The engine is pure growth, the filter is pure refusal. Only together do they say: check first, then feed.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's the layout. A kitchen table, a sheet of paper, one line for each habit. Each line gets the question, and every answer goes in pencil, so you can rub it out when it turns out wrong.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A pencil! After all that talk of sacred orders, you bring a pencil.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a pencil, narrator. It's how you rub things out. Stop feeding the lines that never reached a carter. The table fills slowly with the few that did.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the polish?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Gets the rubber. A little more every week. I'm not stopping you polishing your own hooks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You've hidden something in this design, March. I can always tell. A bit of it that's only for you.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Not telling you that one. Keep your nose out of the drawer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You've beaten me again, March, and I shall lodge a complaint with the mast. The mast has heard worse from better.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I beat you fair. Now go back to the start. You already know which habit is the one that never sold. Say it to yourself, quietly.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes, yes, March, you had me pinned before I'd finished the bowl. It's gone one in the morning, the kettle's cold, and I was wrong to think the clock was harmless.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next, Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions. Bring the pencil.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The crow has the final croak tonight, and the mast can carry the complaint for me.

segments.title: THE BELL THAT WENT OFF EARLY
notes: Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions
segments.angle: What would this idea look like if I went to its extreme? Could that open up anything interesting?

sources.text: Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: When you say you're gonna do something, you gotta follow it through.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: It does more for your self-belief to say you'll meditate for 10 minutes and actually do 10 minutes vs saying you'll do 30 minutes and only doing 20 minutes.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: Every action you take should be intentional and deliberately thought out.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You set a timer for 10 minutes. You'll sit still for every one of them. Then, a few breaths in, you catch yourself half hoping the bell goes off early.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, March, you open on a bell, and I shall answer with a whole choir.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The common belief runs like this: living by design means every hour is booked before it arrives. Nothing left to chance. The fuller the diary, the nobler the soul. Sing it as a hymn, if you like.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the lie is: plan every minute and you're virtuous.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Booked solid. And proud of it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Booked solid, and you don't dare breathe outside the lines. Now the claim, read whole: 'When you say you're gonna do something, you gotta follow it through.' Simple as that, says the note.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't you dare call it simple, narrator. That sentence has broken more good plans than the weather.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall hold the best part back, the comparison further down the note, until we're sat at the table. You'll want it more for waiting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So keeping a small promise to yourself counts for more than a big one you break.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Not counts for more. Makes your words mean anything at all. A promise you break to yourself teaches you to spend your own word cheap...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: ...and a cheap word buys nothing. Yes, I heard the note.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. Then let's say. Kitchen clock on the wall, timer set for 10 minutes, the biscuit tin lid off beside it so I can see the lid. I write it on the sheet in pencil: 10 minutes. Then I sit.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the tick, March. Put the tick beside it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Tick. In pencil. 10 minutes kept.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Beside it, the line I wrote in my head, the one nobody can see: 30 minutes, sitting like a monk until the lunch bell.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the tick is worth more than the 30 you dreamed up. The dream costs nothing and never gets sat. It's a simple sum.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple? It took me a whole timer to see that. Don't call it simple.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then admit I'm right about the tick.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, you're right. Anyway. The timer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here is the hard part, and I'm not going to soften it for you. Most of the 30 minutes people dream of will never be sat in.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The dream feels like virtue. It asks nothing of you. That is its whole trick.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the dream is the cheap habit wearing a robe.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes. Now go to the extreme, since you've been itching for it. The note says every action should be intentional and deliberately thought out. Then the nap is on the sheet, the wasted afternoon is on the sheet, the long lean against a wall with nothing to show for it. All of it timed, all of it with a purpose.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Scheduled naps, narrator. Honestly.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the crow on the mast is no longer a bird. It's a scheduled event with a purpose, a line item on the sheet. I shall lodge that complaint with the mast at once.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The crow has croaked at the same hour for years, narrator.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's a habit, not a design.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The mast will take that poorly.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Predictable is not the same as designed. The crow keeps an appointment it never made. Nobody wrote the crow a sheet.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's just there at the hour, every day, and nobody's ticking it off.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And we do much the same, March. The habit nobody chose still runs at its hour...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't go grand on the crow.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: ...and we call the running a plan. I'm being honest. The crow shows the difference, and that's why I came to it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So here's the fork. Same kitchen table, one page between them.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Go on, then.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The first has a line for every breath. Wherever the day slipped, a line gets rubbed out, and they sit there tense, always correcting, never finished.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the other one?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The other has made a few small promises and keeps them. They sit back relaxed, because their word is already the plan. Their page has a handful of lines, and none of them is rubbed out.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The first one is a clerk. The other is at rest. I know which I'd rather be.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ooh, a clerk. Harsh.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Back to the bell. The early bell was the first broken promise, before you'd even sat down.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Half hoping was the crack.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Mast, lodge this: March was right about the bell. Right from the start, and I shall not hear the end of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Write it on the sheet, narrator. In pencil.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes, yes. The bell went first.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next up, Remove Negatives Over Adding More Positives and Failure Is How We Learn And Grow. Bring a rubber.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The crow gets the last word, as usual. It is the small hours, and the tea has gone cold again.
